body: It was 11.00 am on a sunny morning in May 2002. I was playing in the wide-open coconut farm just outside my home.
Mom called me out loud, "Son, come here. Postwoman just delivered a post for you"

Leaving the toys behind, I ran towards her. It was a heavy white envelope. I opened it carefully and found a bunch of documents written in English. I was a Malayalam medium student, who had started learning English alphabets and simple words just a year before. I couldn't figure out what was written in it. The only person I could think of for decyphering such a complicated letter was Sritha chechi, who was a graduate student then.

Fixing the buttonless trousers with a safety pin, I sprinted to Madhavan uncle's house. Sritha chechi is Madhavan uncle's daughter. I was happy that she was home then. I briefed her about the letter and my incompetency to decode it. Sritha chechi glanced through the letter and with amazement and a smile, she congratulated me! "Yes little champ, you have got admission to Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalaya, Mayannur!"

I was trying to recollect the JNV entrance exam I wrote at Valappadu High School in January or February of that year. And I was curious to know about the rest of the content in the letter. She read it in detail and, with a bit of surprise, told me, "Today is the last day to report to the principal that you are accepting the admission letter!"

I didn't even have a clue where on the earth JNV Thrissur is located. I could understand from the letterhead that it was a place called Mayannur. Even Sritha chechi didn't have any idea of that place.

I rushed back home and informed mom about the letter's content in a single breath. Obviously, she, a homemaker for two decades, hardly went out to any place outside home town didn't know about the place either. Being a road construction worker, my father would have known about this place, but unfortunately he had gone to work and there was no means to connect to him.

Then my sister had an idea. "Shall we ask Absar ikka about this place?" Absar ikka was the neighbour we had who had explored the 'outer world'. He was indeed a hero to us. There were no land or mobile phones in our village then. I had to borrow my friend's bicycle to search for Absar Ikka. I found him in the nearby autoland. Fortunately, he had already been to this place, Mayannur. From his explanation, I got to know that this place is too far from my hometown. Such an altruist, understanding my helplessness he immediately agreed to accompany me and mom to JNV Mayannur.
By 2.00 pm, we had lunch and set out for JNV.

Courtesy : maps.google.com The long journey by 3 or 4 public transport buses ended in the evening 6.30 pm, at the JNV Bus Stop, I don't remember the name of the bus stop. Sun had already set in the hilly place long back. It was dark and some sort of insecurity started growing in young me. The painful sob of a passenger train crept into my ears. It seemed that the train was just reciprocating the feelings of its passengers who were leaving their homeland for finding a living.

Three of us started walking towards JNV campus. After 20-25 mins walk from the bus stop, there I could see the board, 'Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalaya Thrissur. The concertina and barbed wires above the compound wall secluded the place from outside. Or was it shattered glass pieces pointing upwards? I am unable to recollect.

Courtesy : www.navodaya.gov.in Seeing the admission letter, the security person let us in and guided us to the Principal's residence. Even though it was very late in the evening, well outside office hours, the principal, Smt Padmini Thankappan was kind enough to listen to us. In the nominal roll, she checked against my name. I am about to be a JNVian.
But my morale to join JNV had already gone. The campus seemed to be very gloomy to me. The tiring journey, twilight, and deserted paths had set a disturbing backdrop in the mind of 10-year-old me.

We started our return and it was quiet a journey! By the time we reached the bus stop, it was close to 7.30 pm. The last bus to the nearby town, Ottappaalam had already left. There was a mom n pop store nearby. The shopkeeper informed us that there won't be any buses further. To reach Ottappalam, there is only one way. "You have to cross the Bharathappuzha River by walk! Since monsoon hasn't onset, the river is comparatively shallow here". (Mayannur bridge was constructed long after this)

The small me was scared. We need to cross one of the biggest rivers in Kerala, about which I had only studied in the social science textbook! I had also known that the river is notorious for flash floods due to extensive damming at many locations. Absar ikka lifted me on his shoulder. I was much worried about my mom. She was only 4.5 feet tall. How could she cross the river? There could be some deep patches which we cannot see in the dark. And people had done localised damming with sandbags. What if she slips over it? There would be undercurrents and we may not even find a trace of her later. This was adding fuel to my already established dislikedness.

It took around 30 to 40 minutes for us to cross the river. Even the three-and-a-half-feet-deep water was more than sufficient to drench her. But we were so fortunate that no flash floods came in between. We reached the ottappalam bus stand. The last bus was set to leave. There were only a couple of seats empty on the bench next to the engine. The bus was going to a place called 'Guruvayoor', which again was 35 km away from home. The only idea was to reach to the closest place as soon as possible.

We deboarded the bus at 'Guruvayoor'. The bus stand was deserted. The buses had done with their trips for the day. How do we reach home now? Staying at the bus stand is not at all safe. There isn't enough money to stay in a hotel room. Absar ikka had an idea. There are many long-distance trucks passing by the highway NH-17. There would be some kind driver who is going to offer us a ride. The hope was not in vain. A blue Swaraj Mazda truck stopped in front of us. Asking no questions, the driver let us into his cabin. We three, along with the driver sat in the cabin. He dropped us in a place which was just 4 km away from my home, and didn't even take a penny!
We started walking at midnight. After an hour of walking, we reached home. The enthusiasm to join JNV had died down in me. I decided to continue with my academics at the nearby primary school.
In hindsight, I understand that it was the biggest blunder of my life! There weren't any people around me or my parents who knew the value of JNV education. If so, my life would have been different!
